# Results — Study 921 (Bill Ladder vs ETF) on the real daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The instrument: a **simulated**
rolling **13-rung, 3-month Treasury-bill ladder**, one rung bought every 7 calendar days and
held to maturity, priced off **^IRX** (the CBOE 13-week bill **discount** quote, converted to
a bond-equivalent yield — see below). **The ladder leg is modelled, not traded**: ^IRX is a
secondary-market quote and a **PROXY** for the auction stop-out a real ladder would receive,
and no execution is charged in the headline. Only the ETF legs are a traded tape. It is
raced against the **total return** of three cash
ETFs (`yfinance`, `auto_adjust=True`, so the monthly distributions are reinvested). Cash is
the numeraire, so nothing is measured excess of anything: the statistic is the annualised
return gap `ladder − ETF` in **bps/yr**. Exactly one execution lag — the quote seen at the
close of day `t` prices the bill bought at `t+1`. As-of **2026-06-30** (the partial current
month is dropped).*

## Data stamp

| Legs | Window | n days | Rolls | Fingerprint |
|---|---|--:|--:|---|
| ^IRX (13-week bill quote), BIL (cash ETF) | 2007-05-31 → 2026-06-30 | 4,799 | 992 | Fingerprint `1e3d76fa1bfa` |

Cross-checks: SGOV (2020-06-02 →, the cheap modern competitor) and SHV (≤1-year Treasuries,
the **duration control** — not a pure bill fund).

## The rate conversion (stated, because it is worth ~9 bps)

^IRX is a **bank-discount** rate on a 360-day basis, not a yield. The study converts it:

```
P   = 1 − d × 91 / 360           (price per 1 of face)
BEY = (1 − P) / P × 365 / 91     (bond-equivalent, actual/365)
```

At a 3.70% quote that is **+8.7 bps**; at a 0.50% quote, **+1.1 bps**. Since the whole
effect under test is ~13 bps, the entire race is also re-run on the **raw** quote (treating
^IRX as if it were already a yield) as a deliberately conservative floor.

## The race — ladder vs cash ETF, total return vs total return

| Fund | Window | n | Ladder CAGR | ETF CAGR | Gap (bps/yr) | HAC *t* | naive *t* |
|---|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **BIL** (1-3 month bills, ER 13.54 bps) | 2007-05-31 → 2026-06-30 | 4,799 | **1.4928%** | 1.3616% | **+12.83** | **+2.75** | +1.15 |
| SGOV (0-3 month bills, ER 9 bps sticker) | 2020-06-02 → 2026-06-30 | 1,527 | 2.9855% | 2.9571% | +2.76 | +0.62 | +0.26 |
| SHV (≤1-year Treasuries, ER 15 bps) | 2007-01-12 → 2026-06-30 | 4,894 | 1.5639% | 1.5801% | −1.65 | −0.34 | −0.21 |

### The inference audit — because HAC *helps* us here

The HAC *t* (+2.75) is more than double the naive *t* (+1.15). When a correction moves the
result the author's way, it has to be audited rather than asserted, so all three questions
are answered below.

**1. Why the naive *t* is wrong.** The lag-1 autocorrelation of the daily difference is
**−0.366** — the Roll (1984) bid-offer-bounce signature. A bill ETF's close oscillates
between bid and offer, so the difference is a first difference of a stationary pricing error
plus a drift; the i.i.d. standard error therefore **over**states the uncertainty.

**2. The knobs, disclosed.** HAC has a bandwidth and the bootstrap has a block length, and
on this tape *both* knobs push the same way — more lags, more significance:

| naive | HAC 1 | HAC 2 | HAC 5 | **HAC 9 (automatic rule, headline)** | HAC 21 | HAC 63 | HAC 252 |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| +1.15 | +1.44 | +1.73 | +2.21 | **+2.75** | +3.45 | +5.54 | +9.26 |

The automatic bandwidth sits near the **bottom** of that range, so the headline is the
conservative member of the kernel family and not a flattering pick. Bootstrap blocks behave
the same way: 5d gives [+1.15, +24.07] (1.8% of draws negative), 10d [+3.74, +22.19], 21d
[+5.32, +20.46], 63d [+8.37, +17.25] — the CI excludes zero at every block length, and the
shortest block is again the least favourable.

**3. The arbiter, which has no knob at all.** Sum the daily difference into
**non-overlapping** calendar periods. The bounce telescopes away inside each period; the
accrual gap accumulates; consecutive sums are near-independent, so an ordinary one-sample
*t* is valid with nothing to choose:

| Aggregation | periods | mean gap | *t* (ordinary, no bandwidth) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Weekly | 997 | +0.246 bps | **+2.18** |
| Monthly | 230 | +1.064 bps | **+3.27** |
| Quarterly | 77 | +3.179 bps | **+3.54** |

**The knob-free test agrees with HAC, not with the naive *t*.** This — not the kernel — is
what the Real stamp rests on. On the conservative raw-quote convention the same test gives
weekly +1.60, monthly **+2.41**, quarterly **+2.60**: still clear at monthly and above,
and honestly short of 2 at weekly.

**Annualised vol:** ladder 0.15% vs BIL 0.49%. This is **not** risk reduction. A
held-to-maturity ladder is carried at amortised cost and never marked; the ETF is marked
every afternoon. The ladder is the same credit, the same tenor and *less* liquid. No Sharpe
race is quoted here for exactly that reason — the denominator would be an accounting
convention.

## Is the gap the fee? (gross-of-fee attribution)

Expense ratios are a **PROXY** — sponsor-published stickers, not tape. The decomposition
adds each fund's ER back to its net return and asks what is left over.

| Fund | Ladder | ETF net | + ER | = ETF gross | Residual |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **BIL** | 149.3 bps/yr | 136.2 | 13.54 | 149.7 | **−0.4** |
| SGOV | 298.6 | 295.7 | 9.00 | 304.7 | −6.2 |
| SHV | 156.4 | 158.0 | 15.00 | 173.0 | −16.6 |

The BIL residual is **−0.4 bps/yr**: the ladder earns what BIL earns *before fees*, to
within half a basis point over nineteen years. There is no curve pickup, no tenor bonus, no
skill — the entire gap is the expense ratio and nothing else. SGOV's −6.2 bps residual says
its *effective* whole-period fee was nearer 3 bps than the 9 bps sticker (it has been
repriced since its 2020 launch), which is exactly why its measured gap is only +2.8 bps.
SHV's −16.6 bps is the duration control working: it holds out to a year and earned a curve
pickup the ladder cannot.

## Block bootstrap CI on the gap vs BIL (2,000 draws, 21-day blocks)

| Gap | 95% CI | share < 0 |
|--:|--:|--:|
| **+12.83 bps/yr** | **[+5.32, +20.46]** | 0.05% |

## Robustness — three eras

| Era | n | mean 13-week quote | Gap (bps/yr) | HAC *t* | knob-free monthly *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 2007-05-31 → 2015-12-31 | 2,163 | 0.49% | +10.46 | +1.03 | +1.32 |
| 2016-01-04 → 2021-12-31 | 1,510 | 0.93% | +14.17 | +3.23 | +4.02 |
| 2022-01-03 → 2026-06-30 | 1,126 | 3.97% | +15.61 | +2.04 | +2.96 |

The **sign** is positive in all three and the slabs partition the sample exactly (no warmup
lost) — but "positive in all three eras" must not be read as three endorsements. Only eras 2
and 3 are **individually significant**; era 1 (2007-2015, 45% of the sample) is
directionally right and nothing more, on either statistic. It is also the era where a bill
ETF's pricing was most chaotic (2008-09) and where the level of rates left the least room to
measure a 13 bps fee. The full-sample result is not driven by era 1, nor contradicted by it.

## Robustness — by rate *level* (the cleanest fee test)

| Regime | n | mean quote | Gap (bps/yr) | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Zero-rate (quote < 1.00%) | 2,785 | 0.15% | +12.64 | +1.94 |
| Normal-rate (quote ≥ 1.00%) | 2,014 | 3.23% | +13.08 | +1.68 |

**The gap is flat in the level of rates.** That is the signature of a fee: a fund charges
13.5 bps whether bills yield 5 bps or 5%. A curve- or carry-driven gap would scale with the
rate level; this one does not move at all.

## Robustness — assumptions and construction

| Check | Gap (bps/yr) | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|
| Discount → bond-equivalent (headline) | +12.83 | +2.75 |
| **Raw quote, no conversion (conservative floor)** | **+9.44** | **+2.02** |
| 4 rungs (monthly roll) | +12.79 | +2.74 |
| 13 rungs (weekly roll, headline) | +12.83 | +2.75 |
| 26 rungs (twice-weekly roll) | +12.82 | +2.73 |

The rate convention moves the gap by 3.4 bps and the rung schedule by 0.04 bps. The verdict
survives the conservative convention, though only just.

## Cost sensitivity — where it breaks

Both frictions are **PROXY / ASSUMPTION**, both swept. 52 rolls a year on 1/13 of NAV means
per-auction friction costs roughly **4×** its per-roll size in annual drag.

| Per-auction friction | Gap (bps/yr) | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|
| 0 bps (TreasuryDirect non-competitive bid) | +12.83 | +2.75 |
| 1 bps | +8.83 | +1.89 |
| 2 bps | +4.83 | +1.03 |
| **3 bps** | **+0.83** | **+0.18** |
| 5 bps | −7.17 | −1.53 |
| 10 bps | −27.16 | −5.81 |

| Reinvestment idle days | Gap (bps/yr) | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|
| 0 (auto-reinvest, settles same day) | +12.83 | +2.75 |
| 1 | +11.21 | +2.40 |
| 2 | +9.59 | +2.05 |
| **3** | **+7.98** | **+1.71** |
| 5 | +4.74 | +1.01 |

**Three basis points of round-trip friction, or three idle days between maturity and
reinvestment, is enough to erase the whole edge.** A TreasuryDirect ladder with
auto-reinvestment pays neither; a brokerage secondary-market ladder pays both.

## Synthetic control (machinery proof only, never supports the stamp)

A mean-reverting short-rate world with a cash ETF charging a *known* fee:

- **Planted 13.5 bps fee, 8 seeds:** recovered **+13.35 bps/yr** (sd 0.53).
- **Free-ETF null, 8 seeds:** recovered **−0.16 bps/yr** (sd 0.53); |gap| ≥ 4 bps in **0/8**.

The pipeline neither invents a fee nor eats one, so the +12.8 bps measured against BIL is a
property of the tape, not of the harness.

## Verdict

- **Signal — Real.** The modelled ladder out-accrues BIL by **+12.83 bps/yr**. The
  significance survives the only test with no tuning knob in it — **non-overlapping** period
  sums at *t* = **+2.18 / +3.27 / +3.54** (weekly / monthly / quarterly) — which is what
  actually carries the stamp; HAC (+2.75) and the block bootstrap ([+5.3, +20.5], 0.05% of
  draws negative) merely concur, and the naive daily *t* of +1.15 is understood to be too
  small because the difference has a lag-1 autocorrelation of **−0.37** (Roll 1984). The gap
  is **flat in the level of rates** (+12.6 vs +13.1), invariant to the rung schedule, and
  survives the conservative rate convention (+9.44, monthly *t* = +2.41). The gross-of-fee
  attribution nails the mechanism: the residual against BIL is **−0.4 bps/yr**, so the gap
  is the expense ratio and nothing else. The synthetic control recovers a planted fee
  (+13.35) and is silent on the null (−0.16, 0/8). **Honest caveats, all named:** the ladder
  leg is *simulated* off a secondary-market quote rather than traded; era 1 (45% of the
  sample) is positive but not individually significant; the raw-quote floor clears at
  monthly and above but not at weekly (+1.60); and the effect is 13 bps — real, mechanical,
  and small. This is an **accounting identity confirmed on the tape**, not a discovery.
- **Tradability — Fragile.** The headline charges **no friction to either leg** — the ladder
  transacts at the mid of a quote it could not actually hit, and the ETF pays no spread on
  the (single) purchase. The edge is exactly a fee, so it caps at whatever the fund
  charges — and it dies at **3 bps** of per-auction friction (*t* = +0.18) or **3 idle days**
  per roll (*t* = +1.71). Worse, the same 13 bps is available for two clicks: against
  **SGOV** the ladder's gap is **+2.76 bps/yr** (*t* = +0.62), i.e. buying the cheaper fund
  captures nearly all of it with none of the 52-auctions-a-year operational burden. And the
  ladder's flattering 0.15% volatility is amortised-cost accounting, not safety — you have
  bought illiquidity, not risk reduction.
- **Survivorship.** No cross-section here, so no classic survivorship bias; but BIL, SGOV
  and SHV are three funds that *survived*, and closed cash ETFs (which tend to be the
  expensive ones) are absent. That omission would, if anything, make the average fund's fee
  larger — it biases *toward* the ladder, not against it.
